overview: Natchez communities in the lower Mississippi region combined farming with ceremonial mound centers. Their autonomous settlement districts were not governed as one centralized monarchy.

items.text: Farmers grew maize, beans and squash, alongside hunting, fishing and gathering. Families lived across a dispersed farming landscape.
The hereditary Great Sun held ceremonial prominence, but settlement district chiefs retained autonomy.
Matrilineal moieties organized reciprocal obligations and marriage relationships, while competing in games such as stickball.
Communities constructed and maintained flat-topped ceremonial mounds. The Grand Village served as a major ceremonial center from 1682 to 1730.
Grand Village mound construction probably began in the thirteenth century, long before its documented colonial-era prominence.
French retaliation after the 1729 conflict forced Natchez people from their homeland. Refugees joined Chickasaw, Creek and Cherokee communities; descendants continue in Appalachia and Oklahoma.
